segments.title: The Fog and What It Hides

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close, passionate, and occasionally furious reading of what many consider the greatest English novel.
I'm your host, and over the course of this series we'll be moving through Dickens chapter by chapter — tracking the fog, the law, the secrets, and the people ground up by all three.
Today we begin at the beginning — or rather, in the fog that Dickens places at the very centre of his world.
Three extraordinary readers have joined me for this journey, and I want to introduce each of them properly.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian whose work reads Bleak House as nothing less than an anatomy of class power.
Every institution in this novel — Chancery, the law, philanthropy — is, for Daniel, a mechanism for protecting the rich at the expense of the poor.
He brings rigour, controlled fire, and an argument Dickens himself might have been startled to hear — that the novel is more radical than its author knew.
Prof. James Blackstone is a legal historian who specialises in Victorian institutions — he knows what Chancery actually was, what it cost, and who paid.
He connects Dickens' world to the present with dry precision, and his wit is as sharp as his scholarship.
And Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer who has voiced more Dickens audiobooks than perhaps anyone alive.
Oliver comes to the text as a performer — he hears the rhythms, catches the comic timing, and knows exactly which passages Dickens wrote for the voice rather than the page.
He is also, I should warn you, endlessly quotable himself.
Now — the fog.
Bleak House opens on one of the most famous passages in the language — London, Michaelmas term, fog everywhere.
But before we get to the fog itself, I want to start with one of the novel's great presences — a man who seems to carry the fog with him wherever he goes.
Oliver — Mr. Tulkinghorn is your opening brief.
What a gift of a character to begin with.
Tulkinghorn is, I think, one of the most frightening figures Dickens ever put on the page — and he barely moves.
The horror of Tulkinghorn is precisely that nothing adheres to him — not place, not time, not feeling.
Dickens gives us this extraordinary sentence — and I want to read it, because on the page it looks almost unremarkable, but spoken aloud it becomes something else entirely.
"He walks into Chesney Wold as if it were next door to his chambers and returns to his chambers as if he had never been out of Lincoln's Inn Fields."
That parallel construction — the two "as if" clauses — it's the grammar of a man who has erased distance itself from his experience.
Chesney Wold and Lincoln's Inn Fields are the same non-place to him, because everywhere is simply where Tulkinghorn conducts his business.
And then Dickens does it again — "He melted out of his turret-room" — melted, not left, not departed.
The man doesn't move through space — he seeps through it.
What strikes me is that Tulkinghorn's imperviousness to place is inseparable from his function.
He is the keeper of aristocratic secrets — which means he is the instrument by which the ruling class maintains its grip on its own members.
Dickens is precise about this — and Oliver, I think, pointed us directly at it with that word "melted."
Tulkinghorn moves without friction because power has no friction — it simply flows where it needs to go.
And there is a passage that makes this almost chillingly explicit — Dickens tells us he carries family secrets in every limb.
"He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress."
Every crease of his dress — the secrets are not metaphorical, they are literally woven into the fabric of his being and his clothing.
This is the man who services the Dedlock family, who holds Lady Dedlock's secret — and therefore holds her.
The historical reality behind Tulkinghorn is actually more unsettling than the fiction, in some respects.
Family solicitors of this type in early Victorian England held extraordinary informal power — power that was entirely unregulated, entirely personal, and entirely dependent on what they knew.
There was no professional oversight body, no code of conduct with enforcement behind it — you simply trusted your solicitor not to use what he held against you.
Dickens captures exactly this ambiguity — and does so with a sentence that is almost a legal formulation.
"Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his personal secret."
"He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients; he is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself."
He is his own client — that is a precision that any Victorian lawyer would have recognised instantly, and flinched from.
Because the moment your solicitor becomes his own client, you are no longer his principal — you are his material.
"His material" — James, that is absolutely the word.
And what I find endlessly pleasurable about Dickens' Tulkinghorn passages is that the satire is so perfectly embedded you almost miss it.
There's a moment where Dickens describes him arriving — and the physical portrait alone is a small masterpiece of malice.
"Rustily drest, with his spectacles in his hand, and their very case worn threadbare.
In manner, close and dry. In voice, husky and low. In face, watchful behind a blind."
That rhythm — "In manner... In voice... In face" — it's a legal inventory, a schedule of assets.
Dickens is cataloguing him the way Tulkinghorn catalogues everyone else.
And then the sting — "The peerage may have warmer worshippers and faithfuller believers than Mr. Tulkinghorn, after all, if everything were known."
"If everything were known" — four words that are practically the thesis of the entire novel.
That phrase does enormous work — "if everything were known" — because the novel is structured precisely around what is not known, and who benefits from that ignorance.
The fog in the opening pages isn't only meteorological — it is the systemic obscuring of accountability.
Chancery runs on fog — on delay, on complexity, on the impossibility of ever seeing the whole picture clearly.
And Tulkinghorn is one of the fog's primary agents — a man whose power derives entirely from what others cannot see.
What is interesting — and Oliver's reading of that final line confirms it — is that Dickens is not entirely sure Tulkinghorn even believes in the class he serves.
He may be a true cynic — a man who holds the aristocracy's secrets and holds the aristocracy itself in private contempt.
Which makes him, if anything, more dangerous — not a zealot, but a functionary who will do whatever the system requires because the system is what pays.
That tension between service and cynicism is, I think, one of the genuinely modern things about Bleak House.
The Victorian legal system was populated by Tulkinghorns — men whose loyalty was formally to their clients but whose actual power came from knowing far more than any client wanted them to know.
And Chancery was the apex of this — a court so entangled in its own procedures that even its officers had ceased to understand what it was for.
There's a small, dry exchange later in the novel where a character simply asks another whether he is a Chancery suitor — and the weight of that question is almost unbearable.
"I believe you're a Chancery suitor, if I have heard correct?" — said with a kind of hushed recognition, as if identifying someone marked by an incurable disease.
Because in Dickens' world, that is precisely what Chancery does — it marks you, it consumes you, and it never, ever lets you go.
Tulkinghorn as fog — as the system's own shadow, moving silently through both worlds without belonging to either.
There's something almost inhuman about him — and yet Dickens insists we watch him very carefully, because he is indispensable to understanding what the novel is doing.
In our next segment, we turn to the figure at the other end of this world from Tulkinghorn — the boy who has nothing, knows nothing, and is known by no one.
We turn, that is, to Jo.

segments.title: The Law's Machinery and the Poor

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've been circling the great engine at the heart of this novel — the Court of Chancery — and today we're driving straight into its machinery.
What does the law actually do to people? Not in theory — in practice, in the flesh, on the street.
With me, as ever, are three people who've lived inside this novel long enough to have opinions about the wallpaper.
Dr. Daniel Rosen reads Bleak House as an anatomy of class power — every institution a mechanism, every victim a proof.
Prof. James Blackstone knows what Chancery actually was — not as fiction but as legal reality — and the gap between the two is often narrower than you'd hope.
And Oliver Trevelyan has read more Dickens aloud than any person living, and hears in the prose rhythms things the rest of us miss entirely.
James, let's begin with you — because Dickens plants us in that courtroom on the very first page, and the people he puts there are extraordinary.
They are extraordinary, and they are also historically precise — which is the unsettling thing.
Dickens isn't inventing grotesques for effect. He's describing what any visitor to the Court of Chancery in the 1840s would actually have seen.
The little mad woman with her reticule full of paper matches — she was a recognisable type.
Chancery suits lasted decades. Suitors outlasted their own sanity waiting for judgment.
And Dickens catches something legally precise in that passage — the sallow prisoner trying to purge himself of contempt.
That was a real procedural trap. You could be imprisoned for contempt of court in a Chancery matter, and the mechanism for release was so convoluted you might never find your way out.
What Dickens understood — and this is the key thing — is that the system's cruelty wasn't incidental. It was structural.
And then there's Tom Jarndyce, who gave the most precise diagnosis of what the court does to a human being.
"It's being ground to bits in a slow mill; it's being roasted at a slow fire; it's being stung to death by single bees; it's being drowned by drops; it's going mad by grains."
Five separate images of incremental destruction — and Tom Jarndyce eventually shot himself.
That catalogue of slow dying — I want to sit with it for a moment, because it's doing something very specific.
Each image in that list is passive. The suitor isn't destroyed — he is ground, roasted, stung, drowned.
The grammar of the sentence enacts the grammar of the system. Agency belongs entirely to the institution, never to the person inside it.
And who gets destroyed by Chancery? Not the lawyers — they're drawing fees regardless of outcome.
Not the Lord Chancellor — he yawns his way through Jarndyce and Jarndyce with magnificent indifference.
The people destroyed are always the people who had something to lose — land, a legacy, a small inheritance — and couldn't afford to protect it.
The law isn't broken in Bleak House. It's working exactly as designed — for those who designed it.
Daniel is absolutely right — but I'd add that Dickens smuggles the indictment inside a kind of monstrous comedy.
Think about that passage in the court — the lawyers yawning, the reporters who have long since given up, the mad old woman with her paper matches.
Dickens makes you laugh at the absurdity first, and then the laughter curdles into something much darker.
The short-hand writers decamp — Dickens' word — when Jarndyce comes on. Even the press has given up.
Which is why I find the Skimpole passage so brilliantly wicked — Skimpole is the comedy of complicity.
He says — and this is almost too perfectly phrased — that Chancery's abuses are, and I'll quote him directly:
"very agreeable to me" — because they produce a charming young shepherd called Richard who transmutes legal misery into pastoral poetry.
The aesthetic parasite. He won't defend the system, but he'll luxuriate in its by-products.
Dickens despised Skimpole more than almost any character he ever created — and he made him irresistible on the page, which is the most damning thing he could do.
The Skimpole position is historically very recognisable — and not only in the Victorian period.
Every era produces its Skimpoles — people who are not ignorant of an unjust system but have arranged their sensibility so that its injustice arrives as entertainment.
What makes him so lethal as a character is that he's not lying. He genuinely doesn't feel obliged to account for himself.
The Poor Law reformers of Dickens' day faced this constantly — a comfortable class that could see suffering perfectly clearly and had simply decided it was not their problem.
That's a more dangerous enemy than active malice, in some ways. Malice at least acknowledges the stakes.
And the novel shows you the other face of this — not the amiable parasite but the predatory gentleman.
That passage in Leicester Square — Bucket hunting the criminals of the genteel underworld — is Dickens at his most polemical.
He's making a precise class argument: the man in fustian can be bad, but the man in a pin-collar is worse.
Because the gentleman criminal wears his crime as respectability. The system validates him.
Dickens says — and Oliver should read this, it needs the performance —
"he is a more designing, callous, and intolerable devil when he sticks a pin in his shirt-front, calls himself a gentleman, backs a card or colour"
The devil of respectability. That's not a metaphor for Dickens — it's a moral diagnosis.
The rhythm of that sentence is almost liturgical — the repeated 'he is,' the list of vices, the mounting weight.
Dickens knows exactly what he's doing when he opens that chapter — the whole of Leicester Square asleep under its false names, false hair, false titles.
Six uses of 'false' in one sentence. He's tolling a bell.
And the Lady Dedlock world reflects the same falseness — but laundered through fashion.
Dickens describes how she supposes herself inscrutable — and then shows how every tradesman in London has her mapped to the millimetre.
The jewellers, the mercers, the librarian — they talk about her like a product to be placed.
And then comes this magnificent image — those who, in Dickens' words,
"in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput."
The whole aristocracy as a Lilliputian fleet — towed away by their own dressmakers. It's devastating and hilarious at once.
What strikes me across all of this — the court, the suitors, the Leicester Square rogues, Lady Dedlock and her jewellers — is how consistently the novel refuses to locate evil in individuals.
The system is the villain. And yet Dickens gives us these extraordinary people inside it.
In our next segment, we'll look at what that system produces at its lowest level — in the figure of Jo, the crossing sweeper, who may be the most important character in the novel.

segments.title: A Woman's Name in the Dark

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
I'm your host, and today we're going deep into one of the novel's most quietly charged territories — the women of Chesney Wold, and the men who watch them.
With me today are three remarkable guides to this territory.
Dr. Daniel Rosen reads Bleak House as an anatomy of class power — and he'll show us how even the domestic interior at Chesney Wold is a system of control.
Professor James Blackstone brings the legal and institutional history — he knows what Chancery actually was, and what that means for everyone caught inside it.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more Dickens audiobooks than anyone alive — hears the prose the way Dickens intended it: for the ear, not the eye.
We're looking today at a cluster of scenes that circle one another — Krook and his ruinous shop, Sir Leicester and his household, and the watchful, dangerous presence of Mr. Tulkinghorn.
Daniel, let's begin with you — and with Chesney Wold, where a young housemaid named Rosa is singing the praises of Lady Dedlock.
What strikes me first about that housekeeper's-room scene is how perfectly it encodes the ideology of deference.
Rosa doesn't just admire Lady Dedlock — she worships her.
She is so affable, so graceful, so beautiful, so elegant — that cascading 'so, so, so' is the grammar of a person who has never been permitted to form a critical thought about her betters.
But then Dickens gives Mrs. Rouncewell her moment of gentle, almost unconscious resistance.
Listen to how carefully it's hedged — he sets it up like this:

"Heaven forbid that she should say a syllable in dispraise of any member of that excellent family, above all, of my Lady, whom the whole world admires; but if my Lady would only be 'a little more free,' not quite so cold and distant, Mrs. Rouncewell thinks she would be more affable."
That 'Heaven forbid' is doing enormous work — it's the sound of a mind that has internalized its own censorship.
Mrs. Rouncewell can barely permit herself the mildest observation — that Lady Dedlock might be warmer — and yet that observation still gets through.
And what's fascinating historically is that Mrs. Rouncewell has considerable power within Chesney Wold — she is the housekeeper, a figure of real domestic authority.
Yet even she must approach any judgment of Lady Dedlock through three layers of self-deprecation first.
Which brings us, I think, to Sir Leicester himself — because Dickens gives us his portrait of the master-servant relationship with a surgical precision that would make a sociologist weep.
The passage about Sir Leicester's view of his dependents is almost too clean in its diagnosis.
"He supposes all his dependents to be utterly bereft of individual characters, intentions, or opinions, and is persuaded that he was born to supersede the necessity of their having any."
'Born to supersede the necessity' — Dickens is describing a man who has never had to imagine another person's interiority.
That is the aristocratic condition in three words: other people are unnecessary.
And yet — and this is the dry joke — in extremis, it is Mrs. Rouncewell he wants beside him.
That detail about Sir Leicester and Mrs. Rouncewell in distress is one of the most politically compressed moments in the whole novel.
He would say 'Leave me, and send Mrs. Rouncewell here' — feeling his dignity safer with her than with anybody else.
His dignity is safer with the servant than with his peers — think about what that tells you about what the aristocracy actually runs on.
It runs on the competence of the people it systematically refuses to recognize as fully human.
I want to stay with that passage for a moment, because as a performer it's a gift — the rhythm of it is almost musical.
'Stunned — would never recover himself, most likely, except to gasp and die' — Dickens puts that death in a subordinate clause, as a throwaway, and that's where the comedy lives.
The real shock isn't the death — it's Sir Leicester encountering an opinion.
But I think the passage that unlocks all of this — the whole system of Chesney Wold, the whole world of inherited power and accumulated debris — is Krook.
Because Krook holds up a mirror to the real Lord Chancellor, and it's not flattering to either of them.
He lays it out himself, quite cheerfully, with that lantern raised:
"I go to see my noble and learned brother pretty well every day, when he sits in the Inn. He don't notice me, but I notice him. There's no great odds betwixt us. We both grub on in a muddle."
'We both grub on in a muddle' — five words that demolish two centuries of legal mythology.
Krook is the great satirical invention precisely because he is structurally identical to the institution he parodies.
The real Court of Chancery in Dickens' time had cases — I am not exaggerating — that had been running for generations without resolution.
Documents lost, estates consumed by legal fees, families destroyed — and all of it conducted with great ceremony and no apparent embarrassment.
So when Krook says he can't 'abear to part with anything' or permit any 'sweeping, nor scouring, nor cleaning, nor repairing,' he's describing Chancery's actual operating procedure.
And then Dickens gives us that other reading of Chancery — the formal, terrible one — in two words spoken by Tulkinghorn.
"'In Chancery. Between John Jarndyce—'"
He doesn't even finish the sentence — and he doesn't need to.
The name alone carries the weight of irreversible entrapment.
And that brings us to the most dangerous reader of portraits in the whole novel — Tulkinghorn with his glasses at Chesney Wold.
The scene is so controlled it's almost unbearable to perform.
He's standing with his back to the chimney-piece, he turns, he raises his glasses — and then he delivers this:
"Who is this? 'Lady Dedlock.' Ha! A very good likeness in its way, but it wants force of character."
'Wants force of character' — a legal man looking at a painted woman and finding her wanting.
He is, of course, already in possession of a secret that could destroy her — and he knows it, and she knows he knows it, and neither of them says a word about it.
The 'Ha!' is doing more work than almost any other punctuation mark in Victorian fiction.
What Tulkinghorn actually does in that scene is assert ownership — not of the portrait, but of the woman it depicts.
Information is the currency of power in this novel — Tulkinghorn is its richest man.
And notice the social geometry: Sir Leicester born to supersede the opinions of his servants, Tulkinghorn appointed to manage the secrets of his masters.
The whole hierarchy folds in on itself — everyone is surveilled, everyone is managed, everyone is watched.
Surveilled, managed, watched — and yet Lady Dedlock's name still carries a kind of force that none of these men can quite extinguish.
We'll return to that force — and to what happens when the portrait and the secret finally come together — after the break.
Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've spent time in the fog of Chancery and the murk of Tom-all-Alone's, and now we turn to a figure who carries both within him — Richard Carstone.
Richard is gifted, charming, and genuinely loveable — and Dickens destroys him with the slow patience of a natural process.
To examine exactly how, we have Daniel Rosen, who reads Richard as a specimen of what an indifferent system does to its most promising subjects.
James Blackstone, who knows what Chancery actually was — not as metaphor, but as machinery — and what walking into it meant for a young man with expectations.
And Oliver Trevelyan, who hears Richard's ruin the way Dickens scored it — in rhythm, in image, in the ache beneath the comedy.
Daniel, Esther's portrait of Richard is affectionate — and devastating.
Where do you begin with this passage?
I begin with the word "system."
Esther uses it almost casually, but Dickens plants it like a charge.
The system addressed Richard in exactly the same manner as it addressed hundreds of other boys — all varying in character and capacity.
That is not neutral description — that is an indictment.
And what's devastating is that Richard is not a failure by the system's measure — he dashes through his tasks with fair credit and often distinction.
The system produces a kind of brilliance — fitful, dazzling — that is perfectly useless for actual life.
And then Esther gives us the hinge of the whole portrait — here it is:
"They were good qualities, without which no high place can be meritoriously won, but like fire and water, though excellent servants, they were very bad masters."
That antithesis — servant and master — is doing the real moral work of the chapter.
Richard's gifts are real. They simply own him rather than serve him.
And Dickens is very clear about who failed to correct that — not Richard, but the institution formed to educate him.
That antithesis is also beautiful prose, and I don't think we should let the argument swallow the music.
"Like fire and water, though excellent servants, they were very bad masters" — Dickens is writing to be read aloud, and that sentence rings like a bell.
The rhythm is almost proverbial — which is exactly the point.
Esther's voice is always measured, always fair — she will not condemn Richard — and yet the sentence condemns the situation precisely.
What I find interesting — and Jarndyce touches on this himself — is that the novel gives us a counter-example almost immediately.
Jarndyce tells the children about Boythorn's schoolboy heroism — and the tone could not be more different from Richard's portrait.
Listen to how Jarndyce sets it up:

"You must not be surprised to see him take me under his protection, for he has never forgotten that I was a low boy at school and that our friendship began in his knocking two of my head tyrant's teeth out — he says six — before breakfast."
Before breakfast! That detail is pure Dickens — the comic precision that makes the absurdity absolutely real.
And Boythorn's passion — his magnificent, ridiculous excess — is in every way what the system failed to kindle in Richard.
The contrast is instructive, but I want to press on what happens to Richard once the educational failure has run its course and Chancery takes over.
Because by Chapter Thirty-Nine, we're watching a process that the novel understands with almost clinical detachment.
Richard walks out of Symond's Inn into sunshine — Dickens notes there is sunshine there today, that parenthetical hedge is doing a lot of work — and passes under the trees of Lincoln's Inn.
And the narrator lists what those trees have witnessed. Let me read it:

"On many such loungers have the speckled shadows of those trees often fallen; on the like bent head, the bitten nail, the lowering eye, the lingering step, the purposeless and dreamy air, the good consuming and consumed, the life turned sour."
That catalogue is devastating in its accumulation.
The bent head, the bitten nail — these are not metaphors, these are postures Dickens observed in real courts of equity, real waiting rooms.
Chancery was a living institution that ground cases for decades — some suits predated the plaintiffs by a generation.
And the narrator's line — "Chancery, which knows no wisdom but in precedent" — is precise legal satire.
A court that governs entirely by what has been done before can only produce more of the same ruin.
And there is the question Dickens poses directly — "why should one be different from ten thousand?"
It sounds like resignation, but it's actually an accusation.
The institution is designed to reproduce itself — to process human beings into precedents.
Richard is not a tragedy of individual weakness — he is what the system manufactures from promising material.
First the school that couldn't see him clearly, then the profession that couldn't hold him, then the court that will consume whatever is left.
"The good consuming and consumed" — that phrase alone is worth ten critical essays.
I want to come back to something James said — the observation in that passage — because it reminds me of what Dickens does with Jo, a few chapters on.
We've been talking about a young man of good family, good prospects, squandering himself in Chancery — and that is genuinely tragic.
But Dickens then places against that picture a boy with no family, no prospects, no system to educate or ruin him — because no system ever acknowledged him at all.
And the passage with Phil Squod nursing Jo — it has this quality I find almost unbearable to read aloud:
"Both thinking, much, how strangely fate has entangled this rough outcast in the web of very different lives."
"This rough outcast" — two words that contain the whole social verdict passed on Jo without trial, without appeal.
And yet the novel entangles him — makes him matter to Jarndyce and Woodcourt and Trooper George and Phil Squod.
Dickens keeps insisting — even against the system's verdict — that this life is worth grieving.
And that, I think, is where the social history and the literary art converge absolutely.
The Victorian Poor Law classified Jo — and the thousands of real children he represents — as a problem of administration.
The novel refuses that classification.
Richard, meanwhile, the Poor Law would never have touched — he belongs to a different tier entirely.
And yet Dickens traces the same logic of consumption through both lives.
The system devours at every level — it just uses different instruments.
The good consuming and consumed — at every level of the social order, and with a different face each time.
That tension — between the novel's moral insistence and the system's indifference — is going to stay with us as we move deeper into Richard's unravelling.
Daniel, James, Oliver — thank you.
Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' great fog-bound novel apart, layer by layer, to see what's really inside.
I'm your host, and today we begin with the world Dickens built — the streets, the houses, the courts, the grotesques who inhabit them.
Joining me are three people I can think of no one better to have beside me for this journey.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads Bleak House as a precise anatomy of class power — every institution a machine for grinding the poor.
Prof. James Blackstone is a legal historian specialising in Victorian institutions — the man who can tell you exactly what Chancery was, and exactly why it was monstrous.

And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more Dickens audiobooks than any living person — approaches the novel as a performer first, hearing rhythms and timing the page can only suggest.
Let's begin where Dickens begins — with the world itself, its buildings, its streets, the physical matter of the novel.
The thing that strikes you first, reading Bleak House aloud, is that the novel is obsessed with buildings.
Not just as backdrop — they're characters, almost.
Krook's rag and bottle shop, Tom-all-Alone's, Bleak House itself — each one breathes and rots and means something.
There's a marvellous moment early on when Esther first encounters Krook and he writes out letters in the air for her.
He writes 'Jarndyce' — she reads it — then, with that same uncanny speed, he rubs it out and writes 'Bleak House.'
And Dickens gives us this wonderfully compressed line:
"These, in some astonishment, I also read; and he laughed again."
That laugh — odd, rapid, twice repeated — is doing enormous work.
Krook knows something she doesn't, and the building knows something the inhabitants don't — and Dickens lets the laughter carry all of that, without explaining a word.
What I find striking about that scene is the names themselves — Jarndyce and Bleak House — written and erased by this half-mad dealer in rags and bottles.
Krook is the system's unconscious — he collects everything the system produces and discards, and he knows the names that matter.
And what the system produces physically — in brick and mortar, in actual streets — Jarndyce spells out for Esther in one of the novel's most devastating passages.
He is describing property nominally belonging to the Jarndyce suit — streets that Chancery has consumed.

"It is a street of perishing blind houses, with their eyes stoned out, without a pane of glass, without so much as a window-frame, with the bare blank shutters tumbling from their hinges and falling asunder, the iron rails peeling away in flakes of rust, the chimneys sinking in, the stone steps to every door — and every door might be death's door — turning stagnant green."
Blind houses, stoned eyes, death's door — this is not metaphor for atmosphere.
This is Dickens naming the precise, material consequence of a legal system that exists to perpetuate itself.
And then comes the line that should be carved above every court entrance in England: 'These are the Great Seal's impressions, my dear, all over England — the children know them.'
It's worth pausing on what Jarndyce actually means by 'the property of costs.'
In Chancery, the costs of a suit could and regularly did consume the entire estate in dispute.
Solicitors, clerks, copying fees, court fees — each layer of the process generated its own charge, payable before the next layer could proceed.
The street Jarndyce describes is not a novelist's invention — it is a documented reality of what happened to contested estates.
What Dickens adds — and Daniel is exactly right about this — is the moral weight.
He makes you see those rusted railings as a verdict on the system, not merely its side-effect.
The genius of Dickens as a performer — and I mean that word quite literally — is that he never lets the polemic crowd out the comedy.
You have that ravaged street, and then, sixty pages later, you have the Smallweeds descending on Krook's shop like a family of very determined beetles.
And the entire court — this little community of the forgotten — goes collectively mad with speculation.
Dickens says — and this is one of those lines that belongs in a comic anthology —
"Never since it has been a court has it had such a Fortunatus' purse of gossip as in the proceedings at the rag and bottle shop."
A Fortunatus' purse — never emptying, inexhaustible — applied to neighbourhood gossip.
The court imagines guineas pouring from teapots, crown-pieces overflowing punch-bowls — and Little Swills at the pub works it all into his act.
There is a whole micro-economy of fantasy in that community, and Dickens renders it with the loving precision of someone who grew up watching such streets very closely.
The comedy doesn't soften the critique — it sharpens it.
These people are fantasising about hidden treasure because they have nothing.
The only lottery available to them is the rumour of a dead miser's hoard.
Skimpole has a line — Skimpole who is himself a study in how the comfortable classes aestheticise their own uselessness — where he describes Richard Carstone's relationship with Chancery.
He imagines Richard as a young man 'bursting with poetry like a young bud' — bounding over the landscape toward a golden prospect.
And what does Common Sense — this dreadfully practical tax-gatherer figure — do?
He tells Richard the prospect is nothing but 'fees, fraud, horsehair wigs, and black gowns.'
Skimpole calls that painful — but Dickens knows it's the truest sentence in the scene.
Skimpole is a masterpiece of satirical indirection — Dickens using a voice he despises to deliver a diagnosis he endorses.
And the historical reality behind Richard's situation is grimly specific.
Young men with a nominal interest in a Chancery suit were, in the early Victorian period, a documented social category — creditors extended them loans against the prospect of a settlement.
The settlement rarely came, the debts compounded, and the young men were eaten alive by the system they thought would save them.
Dickens knew this from his own family's encounters with debt and imprisonment.
The anger in that novel is not abstract — it is very precisely remembered.
There's a passage in Chapter Thirty-Two that I think about every time I walk past a closed shop late at night.
It's the night before Krook's death — though we don't know that yet — and Weevle is going up and down, up and down, between his room and the street door.
The air itself is the subject — Dickens opens the chapter with this:
"It is a fine steaming night to turn the slaughter-houses, the unwholesome trades, the sewerage, bad water, and burial-grounds to account, and give the registrar of deaths some extra business."
Give the registrar of deaths some extra business — it's almost cheerful, that.
It's the prose equivalent of a man in a top hat gesturing pleasantly at a catastrophe.
And underneath it, Weevle in his tight velvet skull-cap going up and down, not knowing what's in the air — but Dickens knows, and we feel it.
That combination — the civic outrage, the comic grotesque, the gothic unease — is, I think, the defining texture of this novel.
And we've only just crossed the threshold.
In our next segment, we move deeper into the machinery — the law, its operators, and the particular genius of Dickens' legal villains.

segments.title: The Weight of Secrets and Systems

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked — the show that takes Dickens' great dark cathedral of a novel apart, stone by stone.
Today's segment is about the weight of secrets and systems — how Dickens builds an entire world in which institutions and individuals alike are defined by what they conceal.
With me, as ever, are three extraordinary guides to this novel.
Dr. Daniel Rosen reads Bleak House as a precise anatomy of class power — every smile, every flourish, every legal delay in service of a system that grinds the poor and protects the wealthy.
Prof. James Blackstone is our legal historian — the man who can tell you exactly what Chancery was, who it served, and what it cost.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, the voice behind more Dickens recordings than any living soul — comes at the novel through its sound, its rhythm, its theatrical genius.
Let's begin with the law — or rather, with the law's most spectacular monument to itself.
The phrase Dickens gives to Kenge — and it is a phrase that rewards real attention — is almost too perfect.
Kenge uses what the narrator calls his silver trowel — persuasively, smoothingly — and then he delivers this:
"Jarndyce and Jarndyce has been termed, not inaptly, a monument of Chancery practice."
A monument. Not a disgrace. Not a catastrophe. A monument — to be admired from a respectful distance.
The real Chancery of the 1840s and 1850s had hundreds of cases that had outlasted the lives of everyone who initiated them.
Estates consumed entirely in legal costs. Children left destitute by cases their grandparents had begun.
And here is Kenge, with his silver trowel, calling it a monument — as if duration alone were an achievement, as if the wreckage were the proof of majesty.
And that self-congratulation is the system's deepest defence mechanism.
Kenge isn't accidentally pompous. His pomposity is load-bearing.
It sustains the belief that the machinery of Chancery is too grand, too constitutional, too essentially British to be questioned.
And Dickens makes the same argument through Sir Leicester Dedlock — but with even more surgical precision.
Sir Leicester regards Chancery — and Dickens' phrasing here is extraordinary — as:
"a something devised in conjunction with a variety of other somethings by the perfection of human wisdom for the eternal settlement of everything."
The indefiniteness — something, somethings — that isn't ineptness. That is contempt.
The ruling class doesn't need to understand its own institutions. It only needs to believe in them — and to fear what might happen if anyone stopped doing so.
The Wat Tyler comparison is extraordinary, isn't it — and I think it's the passage's real sting.
Sir Leicester's dread isn't that Chancery is expensive or unjust. His dread is that a complaint about it might encourage someone in the lower classes to rise up.
Reform isn't a legal question for Sir Leicester. It is a question of social order — of keeping certain people in their place.
And the most devastating detail — the one that gives Dickens' comedy its acidic edge — is this:
"he has a shadowy impression that for his name — the name of Dedlock — to be in a cause, and not in the title of that cause, is a most ridiculous accident."
He barely knows what the case is about. His concern is the typography.
The typography — yes, that's it exactly. The name of Dedlock must be prominent. The rest is detail.
When you read that passage aloud — and I've read it more times than I can count — the rhythm does all the work.
The mounting clauses — slow, expensive, British, constitutional — each one a little more portentous than the last.
And then — like a pin through a balloon — the revelation that his one actual concern is the billing order.
What interests me equally, though, is that Dickens uses the same technique for Harold Skimpole — but in a completely different register.
Where Sir Leicester is marble-heavy, Skimpole is all air and music.
Listen to how Esther describes him — and this is the passage I can never get out of my head:
"He was speaking of himself as if he were not at all his own affair, as if Skimpole were a third person."
A third person. He has grammatically absented himself from responsibility.
And Dickens is very precise about the mechanism — Skimpole presents his own helplessness as a communal obligation.
His claims — as Esther puts it — are the general business of the community and must not be slighted.
That is exactly what the ruling class does with Chancery. What Sir Leicester does with the name of Dedlock.
The system presents its own appetite as a general necessity. And the rest of us are supposed to service it — gratefully.
The cruelty of Skimpole is that he's genuinely delightful. Dickens makes him enchanting — that is Esther's word, and she means it.
And Esther is not a fool. She sees the confusion — she is honest about the confusion — but she can't quite locate the wrongness.
Dickens gives her this extraordinary sentence — and the punctuation does something remarkable here:
"I was confused by not exactly understanding why he was free of them. That he WAS free of them, I scarcely doubted; he was so very clear about it himself."
That capitalised WAS — in Dickens' own text — is a performer's instruction. Stress it, let it hang.
Because the horror of Skimpole is that his confidence is his alibi.
That connects back to the Lord Chancellor and the naming of Bleak House in court — a moment that sounds almost banal on first reading.
The Lord Chancellor is still turning over leaves — still leafing through papers — when he says it:
"The Jarndyce in question is Jarndyce of Bleak House."
Five words: Jarndyce of Bleak House. And behind them: a family, a fortune, a generation of lives already consumed.
The Lord Chancellor doesn't pause. He turns over leaves. The machinery doesn't even notice what it grinds.

So we have Sir Leicester who won't question the system because the system is the order he depends on, Kenge who flatters it with polysyllables, Skimpole who exempts himself from it by pure force of personality, and the Lord Chancellor who simply doesn't register the human cost.
Different actors, different methods — one system.
Coming up: we follow the human wreckage of that system — and the figure at the very bottom of it, who never had the luxury of a name in any title.
We've spent this episode inside the machinery of Bleak House — its court, its fog, its casualties.
But Dickens doesn't just describe the system — he delivers a verdict on it.
And in this final segment, I want each of you to bring that verdict into focus.
James, let's start with you — because the novel opens with a joke, and the joke is on everyone.
Yes — and it's worth sitting with exactly how Dickens phrases that opening joke, because he means every syllable of it.
He writes, of Jarndyce and Jarndyce:
"Jarndyce and Jarndyce has passed into a joke. That is the only good that has ever come of it. It has been death to many, but it is a joke in the profession."
Death to many. A joke in the profession.
That juxtaposition is not rhetorical flourish — it is a precise description of how legal institutions actually functioned.
The suffering of litigants was professionally invisible — a resource to be processed, not a problem to be solved.
And when reform threatened to interrupt that processing, the profession had its answer ready.
Kenge's defence of Vholes is the most perfectly observed piece of institutional self-preservation in English fiction.
"Sir, that class of practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth."
One sentence. Parliamentary inquiry, ended. Ten years of reform, frozen.
What James has put his finger on is that Dickens understood, deep in his bones, how language protects power.
The Kenge passage is comedy, yes — but it's comedy with a scalpel inside it.
Every time I've read it aloud, you can feel the audience start to laugh and then stop — because they recognise the manoeuvre.
But then there's Gridley — and Gridley is where the comedy cracks open entirely.
"I'll shame them. To the last, I'll show myself in that court to its shame."

"If I knew when I was going to die, and could be carried there, and had a voice to speak with, I would die there, saying, 'You have brought me here and sent me from here many and many a time. Now send me out feet foremost!'"
Feet foremost. That's the phrase that finishes you.
Gridley knows the system will outlast him — and he is determined that it will not outlast his accusation.
Oliver is right that Gridley is the crux — but I think we need to say plainly what Gridley's rage actually is.
It is not the rage of a man who has been treated unfairly by an otherwise fair system.
It is the rage of someone who has finally understood that the system is working exactly as designed — and the design was never for him.
Which is why Richard Carstone's trajectory is, in some ways, the novel's most merciless argument.
Richard is not poor — he has every social advantage — and Chancery destroys him just as thoroughly.
By the end, his mind has been so colonised by the suit that Jarndyce himself — the man who sheltered him — becomes the enemy.
"He becomes to me the embodiment of the suit; that in place of its being an abstraction, it is John Jarndyce."
The suit has replaced reality. The institution has replaced the person.
Dickens understood — perhaps more clearly than his own politics allowed him to say — that this is what total institutional power does to a mind.
What Daniel has described is also, historically, precisely what happened to actual Chancery litigants.
There are case records — not fictional, actual case records — of families in which the suit became the organising principle of three generations of life.
Children grew up knowing they were part of a case before they knew what a case was.
And the reform, when it finally came — the Judicature Act of 1873 — came not from the profession's conscience but from its embarrassment.
Vholes won, in the end, for twenty more years after Dickens published this novel.
Twenty years is actually rather efficient, by Chancery standards.
But what I keep returning to, as a reader — as a performer — is that Dickens doesn't let the novel end in pure fury.
There is grief in it. There is even, in places, something that might be called tenderness toward the doomed.
Gridley's speech is defiance — but it is also the speech of a man who has been broken and knows it and will not pretend otherwise.
That combination — clarity about the system, grief about what it costs — is what makes Bleak House endure.
I'll agree with Oliver on that — and push it one step further.
The reason the novel endures is not that it exposes an old injustice.
It is that the mechanisms it describes — the institutional self-interest, the respectability deployed as a shield, the way process consumes people — are not historical curiosities.
They are the operating system of every large institution in every era.
Dickens named it. We are still living in it.
Dickens named it. We are still living in it — that may be the most honest summary of Bleak House I've heard.
To Daniel Rosen, James Blackstone, and Oliver Trevelyan — thank you for making this novel newly vivid and newly urgent.
Bleak House was published in 1853. It has never gone out of print.
Make of that what you will.

c42:p0.text:
From the verdant undulations and the spreading oaks of the Dedlock
property, Mr. Tulkinghorn transfers himself to the stale heat and
dust of London. His manner of coming and going between the two places
is one of his impenetrabilities. He walks into Chesney Wold as if it
were next door to his chambers and returns to his chambers as if he
had never been out of Lincoln’s Inn Fields. He neither changes his
dress before the journey nor talks of it afterwards. He melted out of
his turret-room this morning, just as now, in the late twilight, he
melts into his own square.
c42:p0.summary: Mr. Tulkinghorn returns from the Dedlock estate to his London chambers with characteristic mystery and detachment, indifferent to the journey and unchanged by it.
c42:p0.best_quote: He walks into Chesney Wold as if it were next door to his chambers and returns to his chambers as if he had never been out of Lincoln's Inn Fields.

c12:p67.text:
At length, one afternoon a little before sunset, when the bright
groups of figures which have for the last hour or two enlivened the
Ghost’s Walk are all dispersed and only Sir Leicester and my Lady
remain upon the terrace, Mr. Tulkinghorn appears. He comes towards
them at his usual methodical pace, which is never quickened, never
slackened. He wears his usual expressionless mask—if it be a
mask—and carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every
crease of his dress. Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great
or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his
personal secret. He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients;
he is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself.
c12:p67.summary: At sunset, Tulkinghorn finally appears, moving at his usual methodical pace with an expressionless mask, embodying mystery and unknown knowledge.

Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his personal secret. He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients; he is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself.

This reply is cut short by Mr. Tulkinghorn’s arrival. There is no
change in him, of course. Rustily drest, with his spectacles in his
hand, and their very case worn threadbare. In manner, close and dry.
In voice, husky and low. In face, watchful behind a blind; habitually
not uncensorious and contemptuous perhaps. The peerage may have
warmer worshippers and faithfuller believers than Mr. Tulkinghorn,
after all, if everything were known.

c24:p65.text:
“Not much of that, sir, though that HAS happened. Mostly they come
for skill—or idleness. Six of one, and half-a-dozen of the other. I
beg your pardon,” said Mr. George, sitting stiffly upright and
squaring an elbow on each knee, “but I believe you’re a Chancery

c24:p65.summary: George confirms such incidents have happened and asks Jarndyce about his involvement in Chancery litigation.

c1:p6.text:
Who happen to be in the Lord Chancellor’s court this murky afternoon
besides the Lord Chancellor, the counsel in the cause, two or three
counsel who are never in any cause, and the well of solicitors before
mentioned? There is the registrar below the judge, in wig and gown;
and there are two or three maces, or petty-bags, or privy purses, or
whatever they may be, in legal court suits. These are all yawning,
for no crumb of amusement ever falls from Jarndyce and Jarndyce (the
cause in hand), which was squeezed dry years upon years ago. The
short-hand writers, the reporters of the court, and the reporters of
the newspapers invariably decamp with the rest of the regulars when
Jarndyce and Jarndyce comes on. Their places are a blank. Standing on
a seat at the side of the hall, the better to peer into the curtained
sanctuary, is a little mad old woman in a squeezed bonnet who is
always in court, from its sitting to its rising, and always expecting
some incomprehensible judgment to be given in her favour. Some say
she really is, or was, a party to a suit, but no one knows for
certain because no one cares. She carries some small litter in a
reticule which she calls her documents, principally consisting of
paper matches and dry lavender. A sallow prisoner has come up, in
custody, for the half-dozenth time to make a personal application “to
purge himself of his contempt,” which, being a solitary surviving
executor who has fallen into a state of conglomeration about accounts
of which it is not pretended that he had ever any knowledge, he is
not at all likely ever to do. In the meantime his prospects in life
are ended. Another ruined suitor, who periodically appears from
Shropshire and breaks out into efforts to address the Chancellor at
the close of the day’s business and who can by no means be made to
understand that the Chancellor is legally ignorant of his existence
after making it desolate for a quarter of a century, plants himself
in a good place and keeps an eye on the judge, ready to call out “My
Lord!” in a voice of sonorous complaint on the instant of his rising.
A few lawyers’ clerks and others who know this suitor by sight linger
on the chance of his furnishing some fun and enlivening the dismal
weather a little.
c1:p6.summary: The court contains a miscellany of tragic figures: a mad woman with paper-match 'documents,' a prisoner repeatedly attempting to clear contempt charges, and a ruined suitor from Shropshire who periodically appears to plead to an indifferent Chancellor.

c5:p56.text:
“Aye!” said the old man, coming slowly out of his abstraction. “Yes!
Tom Jarndyce—you’ll excuse me, being related; but he was never known
about court by any other name, and was as well known there as—she is
now,” nodding slightly at his lodger. “Tom Jarndyce was often in
here. He got into a restless habit of strolling about when the cause
was on, or expected, talking to the little shopkeepers and telling
’em to keep out of Chancery, whatever they did. ‘For,’ says he, ‘it’s
being ground to bits in a slow mill; it’s being roasted at a slow
fire; it’s being stung to death by single bees; it’s being drowned by
drops; it’s going mad by grains.’ He was as near making away with
himself, just where the young lady stands, as near could be.”
c5:p56.summary: Krook relates the tragic story of Tom Jarndyce, the original plaintiff in the suit, who repeatedly warned others to avoid Chancery's destruction. Tom became suicidal and eventually shot himself at a tavern near Chancery Lane.
c5:p56.best_quote: For, says he, it's being ground to bits in a slow mill; it's being roasted at a slow fire; it's being stung to death by single bees; it's being drowned by drops; it's going mad by grains.

c37:p43.text:
“My dear Miss Summerson, here is our friend Richard,” said Mr.
Skimpole, “full of the brightest visions of the future, which he
evokes out of the darkness of Chancery. Now that’s delightful, that’s
inspiriting, that’s full of poetry! In old times the woods and
solitudes were made joyous to the shepherd by the imaginary piping
and dancing of Pan and the nymphs. This present shepherd, our
pastoral Richard, brightens the dull Inns of Court by making Fortune
and her train sport through them to the melodious notes of a judgment
from the bench. That’s very pleasant, you know! Some ill-conditioned
growling fellow may say to me, ‘What’s the use of these legal and
equitable abuses? How do you defend them?’ I reply, ‘My growling
friend, I DON’T defend them, but they are very agreeable to me. There
is a shepherd—youth, a friend of mine, who transmutes them into
something highly fascinating to my simplicity. I don’t say it is for
this that they exist—for I am a child among you worldly grumblers,
and not called upon to account to you or myself for anything—but it
may be so.’”
c37:p43.summary: Richard asks Esther to arrange a private morning walk so he can justify himself and his relationship with John Jarndyce.

c26:p0.text:
Wintry morning, looking with dull eyes and sallow face upon the
neighbourhood of Leicester Square, finds its inhabitants unwilling to
get out of bed. Many of them are not early risers at the brightest of
times, being birds of night who roost when the sun is high and are
wide awake and keen for prey when the stars shine out. Behind dingy
blind and curtain, in upper story and garret, skulking more or less
under false names, false hair, false titles, false jewellery, and
false histories, a colony of brigands lie in their first sleep.
Gentlemen of the green-baize road who could discourse from personal
experience of foreign galleys and home treadmills; spies of strong
governments that eternally quake with weakness and miserable fear,
broken traitors, cowards, bullies, gamesters, shufflers, swindlers,
and false witnesses; some not unmarked by the branding-iron beneath
their dirty braid; all with more cruelty in them than was in Nero,
and more crime than is in Newgate. For howsoever bad the devil can be
in fustian or smock-frock (and he can be very bad in both), he is a
more designing, callous, and intolerable devil when he sticks a pin
in his shirt-front, calls himself a gentleman, backs a card or
colour, plays a game or so of billiards, and knows a little about
bills and promissory notes, than in any other form he wears. And in
such form Mr. Bucket shall find him, when he will, still pervading
the tributary channels of Leicester Square.
c26:p0.summary: The omniscient narrator describes the criminal inhabitants of Leicester Square waking on a wintry morning—swindlers, gamesters, and false gentlemen who are more evil in respectability than in rags.
c26:p0.best_quote: he is a more designing, callous, and intolerable devil when he sticks a pin in his shirt-front, calls himself a gentleman, backs a card or colour, plays a game or so of billiards

c2:p12.text:
Has Mr. Tulkinghorn any idea of this himself? It may be so, or it may
not, but there is this remarkable circumstance to be noted in
everything associated with my Lady Dedlock as one of a class—as one
of the leaders and representatives of her little world. She supposes
herself to be an inscrutable Being, quite out of the reach and ken of
ordinary mortals—seeing herself in her glass, where indeed she looks
so. Yet every dim little star revolving about her, from her maid to
the manager of the Italian Opera, knows her weaknesses, prejudices,
follies, haughtinesses, and caprices and lives upon as accurate a
calculation and as nice a measure of her moral nature as her
dressmaker takes of her physical proportions. Is a new dress, a new
custom, a new singer, a new dancer, a new form of jewellery, a new
dwarf or giant, a new chapel, a new anything, to be set up? There are
deferential people in a dozen callings whom my Lady Dedlock suspects
of nothing but prostration before her, who can tell you how to manage
her as if she were a baby, who do nothing but nurse her all their
lives, who, humbly affecting to follow with profound subservience,
lead her and her whole troop after them; who, in hooking one, hook
all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet
of the majestic Lilliput. “If you want to address our people, sir,”
say Blaze and Sparkle, the jewellers—meaning by our people Lady
Dedlock and the rest—“you must remember that you are not dealing
with the general public; you must hit our people in their weakest
place, and their weakest place is such a place.” “To make this
article go down, gentlemen,” say Sheen and Gloss, the mercers, to
their friends the manufacturers, “you must come to us, because we
know where to have the fashionable people, and we can make it
fashionable.” “If you want to get this print upon the tables of my
high connexion, sir,” says Mr. Sladdery, the librarian, “or if you
want to get this dwarf or giant into the houses of my high connexion,
sir, or if you want to secure to this entertainment the patronage of
my high connexion, sir, you must leave it, if you please, to me, for
I have been accustomed to study the leaders of my high connexion,
sir, and I may tell you without vanity that I can turn them round my
finger”—in which Mr. Sladdery, who is an honest man, does not
exaggerate at all.
c2:p12.summary: Despite believing herself inscrutable, Lady Dedlock is perfectly understood and managed by tradespeople and servants who deliberately lead her and her circle by flattery and careful study of her preferences.
c2:p12.best_quote: who, in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput

c12:p36.text:
That evening, in the housekeeper’s room, Rosa can do nothing but
murmur Lady Dedlock’s praises. She is so affable, so graceful, so
beautiful, so elegant; has such a sweet voice and such a thrilling
touch that Rosa can feel it yet! Mrs. Rouncewell confirms all this,
not without personal pride, reserving only the one point of
affability. Mrs. Rouncewell is not quite sure as to that. Heaven
forbid that she should say a syllable in dispraise of any member of
that excellent family, above all, of my Lady, whom the whole world
admires; but if my Lady would only be “a little more free,” not quite
so cold and distant, Mrs. Rouncewell thinks she would be more
affable.
c12:p36.summary: That evening, Rosa praises Lady Dedlock effusively; Mrs. Rouncewell confirms most of this but privately feels Lady Dedlock could be warmer and more affable.
c12:p36.best_quote: Mrs. Rouncewell is not quite sure as to that...Mrs. Rouncewell thinks she would be more affable.

c7:p7.text:
The present representative of the Dedlocks is an excellent master. He
supposes all his dependents to be utterly bereft of individual
characters, intentions, or opinions, and is persuaded that he was
born to supersede the necessity of their having any. If he were to
make a discovery to the contrary, he would be simply stunned—would
never recover himself, most likely, except to gasp and die. But he is
an excellent master still, holding it a part of his state to be so.
He has a great liking for Mrs. Rouncewell; he says she is a most
respectable, creditable woman. He always shakes hands with her when
he comes down to Chesney Wold and when he goes away; and if he were
very ill, or if he were knocked down by accident, or run over, or
placed in any situation expressive of a Dedlock at a disadvantage, he
would say if he could speak, “Leave me, and send Mrs. Rouncewell
here!” feeling his dignity, at such a pass, safer with her than with
anybody else.
c7:p7.summary: Sir Leicester is an excellent but blind master who denies his servants any individuality, yet ironically trusts and respects Mrs. Rouncewell above all others in distress.
c7:p7.best_quote: he supposes all his dependents to be utterly bereft of individual characters, intentions, or opinions

c5:p42.text:
“You see, I have so many things here,” he resumed, holding up the
lantern, “of so many kinds, and all as the neighbours think (but THEY
know nothing), wasting away and going to rack and ruin, that that’s
why they have given me and my place a christening. And I have so many
old parchmentses and papers in my stock. And I have a liking for rust
and must and cobwebs. And all’s fish that comes to my net. And I
can’t abear to part with anything I once lay hold of (or so my
neighbours think, but what do THEY know?) or to alter anything, or to
have any sweeping, nor scouring, nor cleaning, nor repairing going on
about me. That’s the way I’ve got the ill name of Chancery. I don’t
mind. I go to see my noble and learned brother pretty well every day,
when he sits in the Inn. He don’t notice me, but I notice him.
There’s no great odds betwixt us. We both grub on in a muddle. Hi,
Lady Jane!”
c5:p42.summary: Krook explains his hoarding habits, his affection for old papers and parchments, his refusal to clean or part with anything, and his identification with the real Lord Chancellor. He introduces his cat, Lady Jane.
c5:p42.best_quote: We both grub on in a muddle.

c2:p23.summary: Tulkinghorn begins reading the formal preamble of the Chancery case: 'In Chancery. Between John Jarndyce—'

c39:p87.text:
“A virtue in which few Englishmen are deficient,” observes Mr.
Tulkinghorn. He has been standing on the hearthstone with his back to
the smoked chimney-piece, and now turns round with his glasses to his
eyes. “Who is this? ‘Lady Dedlock.’ Ha! A very good likeness in its
way, but it wants force of character. Good day to you, gentlemen;
good day!”
c39:p87.summary: Tulkinghorn examines Lady Dedlock's portrait, comments cryptically on its weakness of character, and then takes his leave with a polite farewell.
c39:p87.best_quote: Who is this? 'Lady Dedlock.' Ha! A very good likeness in its way, but it wants force of character.

c17:p0.text:
Richard very often came to see us while we remained in London (though
he soon failed in his letter-writing), and with his quick abilities,
his good spirits, his good temper, his gaiety and freshness, was
always delightful. But though I liked him more and more the better I
knew him, I still felt more and more how much it was to be regretted
that he had been educated in no habits of application and
concentration. The system which had addressed him in exactly the same
manner as it had addressed hundreds of other boys, all varying in
character and capacity, had enabled him to dash through his tasks,
always with fair credit and often with distinction, but in a fitful,
dazzling way that had confirmed his reliance on those very qualities
in himself which it had been most desirable to direct and train. They
were good qualities, without which no high place can be meritoriously
won, but like fire and water, though excellent servants, they were
very bad masters. If they had been under Richard’s direction, they
would have been his friends; but Richard being under their direction,
they became his enemies.
c17:p0.summary: Esther reflects on Richard's natural talents being undermined by his lack of discipline, a problem rooted in an educational system that addresses all students identically rather than according to individual capacity.
c17:p0.best_quote: They were good qualities, without which no high place can be meritoriously won, but like fire and water, though excellent servants, they were very bad masters.

c9:p25.text:
“But it’s the inside of the man, the warm heart of the man, the
passion of the man, the fresh blood of the man, Rick—and Ada, and
little Cobweb too, for you are all interested in a visitor—that I
speak of,” he pursued. “His language is as sounding as his voice. He
is always in extremes, perpetually in the superlative degree. In his
condemnation he is all ferocity. You might suppose him to be an ogre
from what he says, and I believe he has the reputation of one with
some people. There! I tell you no more of him beforehand. You must
not be surprised to see him take me under his protection, for he has
never forgotten that I was a low boy at school and that our
friendship began in his knocking two of my head tyrant’s teeth out
(he says six) before breakfast. Boythorn and his man,” to me, “will
be here this afternoon, my dear.”
c9:p25.summary: Mr. Jarndyce explains Boythorn's passionate, extreme nature and his school friendship with him, rooted in Boythorn knocking out teeth of their tyrannical headmaster, setting expectations for his protective behavior.
